title: Week 5 — Dispersion
body:
Hello class,

Couple of housekeeping issues to start:

* if you send me a message via the chat on the site and don't sign it, I have no idea who sent that or how to respond to you. So in the future, if you reach out to me that way, please make sure you tell me who you are and how you'd like me to reach back out to you. 
* I'm still somewhat new to  teaching here, and am definitely new to going rogue hijacking the course site to make it easier (for me) to stay organized, especially getting the lectures recorded and uploaded. That said, if you have any advice or suggestions on how I can make this a better version of the class for y'all, please let me know. I want y'all to get as much as you can in our time together, so if there's something that's stymying that, let me know so there's nothing hindering the learning experience.
* This week being shortened by the holiday, I'll give you info about the midterm next week so you're not burdened with that for the Fourth. I got distracted last week and didn't push an update to the site that I meant to, so this week will just be the work on Averages and watching the week 5 lecture video. 

As for the curriculum:

I uploaded a more current version of the 'Averages' spreadsheet that has the instructions more explicitly written out. This will be due Friday (7/3) at 11:59pm 

This weeks lesson on dispersion is available for viewing. As noted above. No hw assigned yet for this lesson. That said, I'd like everyone to go back to their submissions for the data visualization and make sure that both problems are complete and the graphs are visible in some obvious location in your spreadsheet please. I walked through how to do the first problem in the lecture, and the second problem is very similar to it. Your graphs should look similar to the picture I dropped in the instructions. The responses I've had so far have been.... underwhelming. So since the test is off our plate for a week, I'd like y'all to take this time to sharpen up what you have on hw1 and complete hw2 so we can start strong after the break. 

if you have questions about any of that,  please let me know, and I'll do my best to help you any way I can. 

Finally, my apologies to those of you who emailed over the weekend; I had to deal with some personal matters out of town last week and am just now getting back into the swing of things.

-Holloway

title: Week 3 — Data Visualization
body:
Hello class,

I saw some good insight on the discussion board about income as a discrete versus continuous variable. That one is interesting, because while income can be any amount, that amount is constrained by the lowest denomination of currency one can be paid ($0.01). So discrete in the sense you aren't being paid in fractions of a cent, but continuous in the sense pennies are such a small amount, they serve as the kind of quantifiable metric  we need to measure the income efficiently. One could make the argument either way, I'm glad y'all were able to think critically about that topic. 

This week, we're going to up the ante a little bit. This week is going to be about displaying the data that we're analyzing. Please give yourself plenty of time to work through the lecture and Excel problems. I attached the Excel doc that I use in the lecture videos so you can follow along. Let me know if you have any problems getting the data to work for you on your version of Excel, and I will do my best to get you where you need to be. 

Getting you familiar with Excel is one of my biggest goals in the class, and we will be working in Excel for the rest of our time together, so please try your best to get a good understanding of that application. Microsoft Excel is still the gold standard for F500 companies finance/accounting/risk management functions, so despite the inroads that Google has made with Sheets, etc., familiarity with Excel will take you a long way (especially since a lot of the functions you learn in Excel transfer cleanly to Google Sheets).

I'll be expecting you to complete the Excel worksheet and email me a copy of the completed spreadsheet by this Sunday 6/21 ( by 11:59pm). Take your time, get it right, and I'll be in touch if you have questions or comments. Have a nice day!

-Holloway

title: Welcome to Business Statistics — Summer 2026
body:
Hello class,

Welcome to Business Statistics! I'm really excited to be teaching y'all this semester especially. I feel like the summer terms are way more chill than during the regular fall/spring school year, and 10 weeks I think is a really good amount of time to pick up the material we're going to cover in this course.

Also, since I've been on this renegade mission to dis-spell whatever technological black hole I've been cursed with by Blackboard. Welcome to the new course site of BUSI 2305! I've tried to consolidate a lot of the good stuff here so it's all in one place, uninhabited by ultra gremlins.

Take a look around, get used to where stuff lives. It should be pretty self explanatory, but definitely ask me if you have questions. The syllabus and course schedule are found in the 'about' tab. If you need to reach me, the contact tab links straight to my email and cell.

The first 'lesson' is posted. This first week should be pretty straight forward. We're just going to be going through the Greek alphabet and learning some of those foreign looking letters. Statistics uses about half of the Greek alphabet in its symbols for various metrics, so learning the Greeks has become a fun little way to start off the semester. Knowing these characters will not only be easy points on assignments and tests, but allow you to become familiar enough with the letters so that when we learn about, say, standard deviation, you'll know that the little cursive 'o' looking shape is actually 'sigma', the Greek letter 's', making it make a lot more sense to represent standard deviation than 'weird cursive o thing'. Check out the video accompaniment — you can hear my beautiful booming baritone singing backup for the song.

In addition to the alphabet lesson, I'd like you all to make sure you take care of the following two items:

1. Make sure you have access to Microsoft Excel on your laptop. This can be handled by either making sure you have a version of Windows that includes the desktop version of Microsoft Excel, or by logging into [Office 365](https://www.office.com) using your school account and running the browser version. If you have problems, you should definitely NOT come to me. There are so many different machines running different versions of whatever, that I gave up on trying to troubleshoot any of them but my own. I can help you with everything beyond getting access on your computer, but that part you'll have to figure out yourself, or call the IT department for help.

2. Go back to [Blackboard](https://acconline.austincc.edu/) (I know I was having fun here too, don't worry it will be one of the last times for this class) and introduce yourself in the discussion board by Friday (6/5). THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING ALL WEEK. Why, you ask, is this so important? THIS IS WHAT I USE TO REGISTER ATTENDANCE. It's an online class, so that's the way I can tell the registrar that you 'attended' the class. DO NOT FORGET. I'm tired of having to go take a verbal beatdown from my department chair along with the registrar's office for y'all forgetting this simple task. If you don't participate in the discussion board, YOU WILL BE DROPPED!

The textbook is optional. Part of my crusade to reform the business statistics curriculum involves emphasizing the type of business applications you may face in your career and de-emphasizing, nay — shitcanning, anything that involves doing rote arithmetic on pencil and paper. For this reason (and many others) the textbook has been replaced with my own secret blend of incredibly profound and compelling case studies that we will go through over the course of the... course. For now, focus on getting good with the Greeks, getting access to Excel, and, for the love of all things statistical, the discussion board (by 6/5).

—Holloway

ps — as you admire this next stage of statistical higher learning distilled into a website, please let me know if anything looks broken — links don't work, Greek letters didn't render, etc. — or if you think I could improve it in any way. Y'all are the first class that will have had the (entire) course organized out here in the wild. Good luck!
